::: {.callout-note title="Scope and status"}
This page describes **conceptual and historical empirical-Bayes workflows** in
which posterior marker summaries from one genomic fit are used to construct
annotation-informed priors for a later fit.

The canonical definitions of the current annotation-aware models, the
$P/Q/H/V_b$ architecture, preprocessing contracts, current capability, and the
approved future direction are given in
[Annotation-Informed Priors](annotation_priors.qmd).

Functions whose names end in `_conceptually` are mathematical pseudocode, not
package APIs. Sections explicitly labelled **Conceptual** or **Research
extension** should not be read as current `sblr` functionality.

In particular, current ordinary MT BayesR uses one `joint_pi` simplex, current
MT BayesRC uses the $P\times H$ factorization described in
[MT BayesRC/SBayesRC](mt_bayesrc_sbayesrc.qmd), and learned MT-LV,
annotation-dependent $H$, and annotation-dependent $V_b$ are not current
production models.
:::

# Motivation

A useful way to incorporate functional annotations is to separate two stages:

1. fit a genomic BLR model and summarize the posterior evidence carried by
   individual markers;
2. model how those posterior summaries vary with annotations and use the
   resulting annotation information to construct priors for a later genomic
   analysis.

Schematically,

$$
\text{genomic fit}
\longrightarrow
\text{posterior marker summaries}
\longrightarrow
\text{annotation model}
\longrightarrow
\text{annotation-informed prior}
\longrightarrow
\text{new genomic fit}.
$$

This is an **empirical-Bayes** construction because information estimated from
one posterior analysis is subsequently used to define or tune another prior.

The approach can be useful when:

- prior information should be inspected before entering the genomic sampler;
- annotations overlap and need conditional adjustment;
- one wants to derive fixed marker-specific prior probabilities or variance
  multipliers from a separate analysis;
- external or cross-fitted data are available for prior construction; or
- a staged genomic-to-annotation-to-genomic workflow is scientifically easier
  to diagnose than a fully joint hierarchical model.

The same construction also creates important inferential caveats. If the same
data are used to estimate both the empirical prior and the final posterior,
uncertainty in the first-stage prior construction is not automatically
propagated into the second-stage posterior.

# Notation and implementation names

Let:

- $N$ be the number of individuals;
- $M$ be the number of markers;
- $T$ be the number of traits;
- $X\in\mathbb R^{N\times M}$ be the genotype matrix;
- $y_t$ be the phenotype vector for trait $t$;
- $b_t$ be the marker-effect vector for trait $t$;
- $A\in\mathbb R^{M\times K}$ be a raw marker-by-annotation matrix.

For marker $j$ and trait $t$, let

$$
\widehat b_{jt}
=
\mathbb E(b_{jt}\mid\mathcal D)
$$

denote the posterior mean marker effect and

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{PIP}}_{jt}
=
\Pr(d_{jt}=1\mid\mathcal D)
$$

the marginal posterior inclusion probability under a BayesC-style activity
representation. For BayesR/BayesRC, the corresponding PIP is the posterior
probability of occupying any positive component.

Here $\mathcal D$ denotes the data together with the likelihood/operator
representation used in the genomic fit.

Throughout this Methods page, mathematical cross-products are written
explicitly:

$$
X^\top y_t,
\qquad
X^\top X,
\qquad
y_t^\top y_t.
$$

Likewise, $q_j$ is reserved for the marker-specific **prior variance
multiplier** used in the canonical $Q$ architecture. It is not used as a name
for $X^\top Xb$ or other fitted cross-product quantities.

# First-stage genomic summaries

For trait $t$ and the actual common-sample Gram matrix $C_X=X^\top X$, define
the exact marker-scale residual score

$$
r_t
=
X^\top y_t-X^\top Xb_t.
$$

Therefore,

$$
X^\top Xb_t
=
X^\top y_t-r_t.
$$

This identity provides a link from posterior marker effects to LD-aware genomic
contributions without requiring repeated access to individual-level genotype
data.

Using posterior mean effects,

$$
\widehat v_{g,t}
=
\frac{1}{N_t}
\widehat b_t^\top
\left(
X^\top y_t-r_t
\right)
$$

is a descriptive sample-scaled genomic-variance quantity.

For an approximate fitted operator $\widetilde C_X$ on the cross-product scale,
the maintained operator score is instead

$$
r_{\mathrm{op},t}
=
X^\top y_t-\widetilde C_Xb_t,
\qquad
\widetilde C_Xb_t
=
X^\top y_t-r_{\mathrm{op},t}.
$$

The corresponding plug-in quantity

$$
\widehat q_{g,t}^{(\mathrm{op})}
=
\frac{1}{N_t}
\widehat b_t^\top
\left(X^\top y_t-r_{\mathrm{op},t}\right)
$$

is an operator-relative genomic quadratic. It is a genomic variance only when
$\widetilde C_X$ is a compatible positive-semidefinite operator on the declared
cross-product scale. If the fitted operator can be indefinite, the expression
is only an algebraic likelihood summary.

For two traits $t$ and $s$ observed on one common sample, the exact plug-in
fitted-value covariance is

$$
[\widehat V_g]_{ts}
=
\frac{
\widehat b_t^\top(X^\top y_s-r_s)
+
\widehat b_s^\top(X^\top y_t-r_t)
}{
2N
}
=
\frac{1}{N}\widehat b_t^\top X^\top X\widehat b_s.
$$

This identity requires one common sample of size $N$ and its actual
cross-product $X^\top X$. A declared positive-semidefinite per-observation
target-population genotype covariance $\Sigma_X$ can instead define
$\widehat b_t^\top\Sigma_X\widehat b_s$. It must be compatible with both effect
vectors in marker order, allele orientation, genotype coding, centering,
standardization, target population, and covariance scale. If the same target
operator is represented on a cross-product scale, then

$$
C_X=N\Sigma_X,
\qquad
\frac{1}{N}\widehat b_t^\top C_X\widehat b_s
=
\widehat b_t^\top\Sigma_X\widehat b_s.
$$

The covariance-scale form is not divided by $N$ again. With a merely symmetric
and potentially indefinite approximation, the result is only an
operator-relative bilinear form. A $\sqrt{N_tN_s}$ normalization for different
trait samples is at most descriptive unless a joint cross-sample model or a
declared target-population covariance supplies the missing operator
information.

These formulas are derived in
[Summary Statistics](summary_statistics.qmd). The important point here is that
the same identity can be used to construct marker- and annotation-level
responses for empirical-Bayes modelling.

## Marker-level response quantities

Several first-stage posterior summaries can be used as annotation-model
responses.

### Posterior mean effect

$$
S^{(b)}_{jt}
=
\widehat b_{jt}.
$$

This retains effect sign and scale.

### PIP-scale response

A bounded logit transform can be used:

$$
S^{(\mathrm{PIP})}_{jt}
=
\operatorname{logit}
\left(
\widetilde{\operatorname{PIP}}_{jt}
\right),
$$

where $\widetilde{\operatorname{PIP}}_{jt}$ denotes a numerically bounded
version of the marginal PIP.

This is a transformed posterior summary, not a Bernoulli observation.

### LD-aware genomic contribution

Define

$$
c_{jt}
=
\frac{
\widehat b_{jt}
\left[
X^\top y_t-r_t
\right]_j
}{
N_t
}.
$$

Then one can use

$$
S^{(g)}_{jt}=c_{jt}.
$$

In the exact Gram case, this response includes the fitted LD structure through
$X^\top y_t-r_t=X^\top X\widehat b_t$. Under an approximate fitted operator,
$X^\top y_t-r_{\mathrm{op},t}=\widetilde C_X\widehat b_t$ instead, and the
resulting response is operator relative.

A conceptual R construction using current code fields is:

```r
S_b <- fit0$bm
S_pip <- qlogis(pmin(pmax(fit0$dm, 1e-6), 1 - 1e-6))
S_alloc <- fit0$bm * (fit0$wy - fit0$r) / n
```

# Set-specific genomic contributions

For a marker set or annotation $\mathcal S_k$, define the signed, descriptive
set allocation

$$
\widehat a_{g,k,t}^{(\mathrm{signed})}
=
\frac{1}{N_t}
\sum_{j\in\mathcal S_k}
\widehat b_{jt}
\left[
X^\top y_t-r_t
\right]_j.
$$

Even when $X^\top X$ is positive semidefinite, this allocation can be negative.
Writing $C_X=X^\top X$ and $\mathcal S_k^c$ for markers outside the set,

$$
\widehat a_{g,k,t}^{(\mathrm{signed})}
=
\frac{1}{N_t}
\left(
\widehat b_{\mathcal S_k,t}^\top
C_{\mathcal S_k\mathcal S_k}
\widehat b_{\mathcal S_k,t}
+
\widehat b_{\mathcal S_k,t}^\top
C_{\mathcal S_k\mathcal S_k^c}
\widehat b_{\mathcal S_k^c,t}
\right).
$$

The second term contains signed LD cross-terms with markers outside the set.
For a disjoint partition, the signed allocations sum to the complete fitted
quadratic, but an individual allocation need not be nonnegative.

For overlapping annotations, they should instead be interpreted as
**attributions**. A marker belonging to several annotations contributes to
every set that contains it, so the totals are not additive.

A different, nonnegative quantity is the within-set fitted genetic-value
variance

$$
\widehat v_{g,k,t}^{(\mathrm{within})}
=
\frac{1}{N_t}
\widehat b_{\mathcal S_k,t}^\top
C_{\mathcal S_k\mathcal S_k}
\widehat b_{\mathcal S_k,t}.
$$

It is nonnegative when $C_{\mathcal S_k\mathcal S_k}$ is positive semidefinite.
It omits LD cross-terms with markers outside the set and therefore does not, in
general, partition the complete genomic variance.

A conceptual implementation is shown below. It assumes one common scalar
sample size `n` for all traits in the illustration.

```r
estimate_signed_allocation_by_set <- function(fit, sets, n) {
  if (!is.numeric(n) || length(n) != 1L || !is.finite(n) || n <= 0) {
    stop("`n` must be one finite, strictly positive sample size.")
  }
  if (!is.list(fit)) {
    stop("`fit` must be a list containing matrix fields `bm`, `wy`, and `r`.")
  }
  if (!is.list(sets) || length(sets) == 0L) {
    stop("`sets` must be a nonempty list of marker-index vectors.")
  }

  b <- fit$bm
  xy <- fit$wy
  residual_score <- fit$r

  if (!is.numeric(b) || !is.matrix(b) ||
      nrow(b) == 0L || ncol(b) == 0L) {
    stop("`fit$bm` must be a nonempty numeric marker-by-trait matrix.")
  }
  if (!is.numeric(xy) || !is.matrix(xy) ||
      !is.numeric(residual_score) || !is.matrix(residual_score) ||
      !identical(dim(b), dim(xy)) ||
      !identical(dim(b), dim(residual_score))) {
    stop("`fit$bm`, `fit$wy`, and `fit$r` must have identical matrix dimensions.")
  }
  if (any(!is.finite(b)) || any(!is.finite(xy)) ||
      any(!is.finite(residual_score))) {
    stop("Effect, score, and residual-score matrices must be finite.")
  }

  valid_set <- vapply(sets, function(idx) {
    is.numeric(idx) && length(idx) > 0L && all(is.finite(idx)) &&
      all(idx == floor(idx)) && all(idx >= 1L & idx <= nrow(b)) &&
      !anyDuplicated(idx)
  }, logical(1))
  if (!all(valid_set)) {
    stop("Each set must contain unique integer marker indices within `fit$bm`.")
  }

  operator_b <- xy - residual_score

  out <- matrix(
    NA_real_,
    nrow = length(sets),
    ncol = ncol(b),
    dimnames = list(names(sets), colnames(b))
  )

  for (s in seq_along(sets)) {
    idx <- sets[[s]]

    for (t in seq_len(ncol(b))) {
      out[s, t] <- sum(b[idx, t] * operator_b[idx, t]) / n
    }
  }

  if (any(!is.finite(out))) {
    stop("The signed set allocations are not finite.")
  }

  out
}
```

The local code variable `operator_b` is deliberately used rather than `q`,
because $q_j$ is reserved for prior variance architecture. It equals
$X^\top Xb$ only for an exact Gram representation; under an approximate route
it represents $\widetilde C_Xb$, so the returned allocations are operator
relative.

## Posterior-summary caveat

The expression above combines posterior means and a residual score. In general,

$$
\mathbb E\!\left[
b_{jt}
\left(X^\top y_t-r_t\right)_j
\mid\mathcal D
\right]
$$

is not identical to

$$
\mathbb E(b_{jt}\mid\mathcal D)
\left[
X^\top y_t-
\mathbb E(r_t\mid\mathcal D)
\right]_j.
$$

Therefore signed allocations calculated from posterior summaries should be
described as descriptive plug-in summaries unless the quantity is computed
draw by draw and then averaged. Neither a draw-wise signed allocation nor its
plug-in version is automatically a valid prior variance.

# PIP enrichment

For annotation $\mathcal S_k$, the posterior expected number of active markers
for trait $t$ is

$$
m^{\mathrm{eff}}_{k,t}
=
\sum_{j\in\mathcal S_k}
\widehat{\operatorname{PIP}}_{jt}.
$$

A simple marginal enrichment ratio is

$$
E_{k,t}^{(\mathrm{PIP})}
=
\frac{
|\mathcal S_k|^{-1}
\sum_{j\in\mathcal S_k}
\widehat{\operatorname{PIP}}_{jt}
}{
|\mathcal S_k^c|^{-1}
\sum_{j\notin\mathcal S_k}
\widehat{\operatorname{PIP}}_{jt}
}.
$$

This measures whether marginal posterior activity is enriched in the marker
set. It is not a variance decomposition and it is not automatically a
conditional annotation effect when annotations overlap.

A conceptual implementation is:

```r
estimate_pip_enrichment <- function(dm, sets) {
  out <- matrix(
    NA_real_,
    nrow = length(sets),
    ncol = ncol(dm),
    dimnames = list(names(sets), colnames(dm))
  )

  all_idx <- seq_len(nrow(dm))

  for (s in seq_along(sets)) {
    idx <- sets[[s]]
    bg <- setdiff(all_idx, idx)

    for (t in seq_len(ncol(dm))) {
      out[s, t] <- mean(dm[idx, t]) / mean(dm[bg, t])
    }
  }

  out
}
```

# PIP-weighted genomic contributions

One can also construct the descriptive quantity

$$
c^{(\mathrm{PIP})}_{jt}
=
\frac{
\widehat{\operatorname{PIP}}_{jt}
\widehat b_{jt}
\left[
X^\top y_t-r_t
\right]_j
}{
N_t
}.
$$

This downweights markers with low marginal posterior inclusion probability.

It should not be interpreted as an exact posterior expectation unless the
underlying joint quantity has been evaluated draw by draw. Multiplying
posterior means by posterior probabilities introduces an additional nonlinear
plug-in approximation.

```r
estimate_weighted_vg_by_set <- function(fit, sets, n) {
  b <- fit$bm
  pip <- fit$dm
  xtxb <- fit$wy - fit$r

  out <- matrix(
    NA_real_,
    nrow = length(sets),
    ncol = ncol(b),
    dimnames = list(names(sets), colnames(b))
  )

  for (s in seq_along(sets)) {
    idx <- sets[[s]]

    for (t in seq_len(ncol(b))) {
      out[s, t] <- sum(
        pip[idx, t] * b[idx, t] * xtxb[idx, t]
      ) / n
    }
  }

  out
}
```

# Overlapping annotations

Marginal set summaries are easy to calculate but can be difficult to interpret
when annotations overlap.

Suppose a marker-level response $S_j$ is modeled as

$$
S_j
=
\mu
+
\sum_{k=1}^{K}
A_{jk}\gamma_k
+
\varepsilon_j.
$$

Then $\gamma_k$ describes the association between annotation $k$ and the
response conditional on the other included annotation columns.

Possible responses include:

$$
S_{jt}
=
\widehat{\operatorname{PIP}}_{jt},
$$

$$
S_{jt}
=
\widehat b_{jt}^{\,2},
$$

or

$$
S_{jt}
=
c_{jt}.
$$

For a bounded PIP response, one may instead use

$$
S_{jt}
=
\operatorname{logit}
\left(
\widetilde{\operatorname{PIP}}_{jt}
\right).
$$

The interpretation is conditional on the chosen annotation design and response
transformation. It does not establish that the annotation causes the genetic
signal.

## Simple conceptual regressions

For example:

```r
annotation_lm_g <- function(fit, annot, trait, n) {
  b <- fit$bm[, trait]
  xtxb <- fit$wy[, trait] - fit$r[, trait]

  response <- b * xtxb / n
  A <- as.data.frame(annot)

  lm(response ~ ., data = A)
}
```

or a PIP-weighted regression:

```r
annotation_lm_g_weighted <- function(fit, annot, trait, n, eps = 1e-6) {
  b <- fit$bm[, trait]
  pip <- fit$dm[, trait]
  xtxb <- fit$wy[, trait] - fit$r[, trait]

  response <- b * xtxb / n
  A <- as.data.frame(annot)

  lm(response ~ ., data = A, weights = pmax(pip, eps))
}
```

A fractional-response approximation for PIP is:

```r
annotation_glm_pip <- function(dm, annot, trait, eps = 1e-6) {
  response <- pmin(pmax(dm[, trait], eps), 1 - eps)
  A <- as.data.frame(annot)

  glm(response ~ ., data = A, family = quasibinomial())
}
```

These are analysis-level models of posterior summaries. They are not the same
as the annotation mechanisms implemented directly inside current genomic
BayesC/BayesR/BayesRC samplers.

# Annotation-level Bayesian regression

Instead of an ordinary regression on marker summaries, one can conceptually
fit a Bayesian variable-selection model with annotations as predictors.

Let

$$
S\in\mathbb R^{M\times T}
$$

be a marker-by-trait response matrix derived from the first-stage genomic fit.
A generic annotation-level model is

$$
S=A\Gamma+E_A,
$$

where

$$
\Gamma\in\mathbb R^{K\times T}
$$

contains annotation effects and $E_A$ is the annotation-model residual matrix.

This is a regression **across markers**. It should not be confused with the
genomic regression $Y=XB+E_Y$.

Because markers are correlated through LD, treating the rows of $S$ as
independent observations is an approximation unless the annotation-level
likelihood explicitly accounts for that dependence. LD pruning, weighting,
block-wise models, or cross-fitting may therefore be appropriate depending on
the scientific goal.

## Conceptual annotation-level ST model

For one trait,

$$
S_t=A\gamma_t+\varepsilon_t.
$$

A BayesC-like annotation prior could be written

$$
\gamma_{kt}
=
\delta_{kt}\alpha_{kt},
$$

with

$$
\delta_{kt}
\sim
\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_{\gamma,t})
$$

and

$$
\alpha_{kt}\mid\delta_{kt}=1
\sim
N(0,\sigma_{\gamma,t}^2).
$$

Posterior summaries such as

$$
\mathbb E(\gamma_{kt}\mid S)
$$

and

$$
\Pr(\delta_{kt}=1\mid S)
$$

describe how strongly annotation $k$ explains the chosen marker-level response,
conditional on the other modeled annotations.

This is a conceptual annotation-analysis model, not a current claim that the
public `sblr` fitters accept arbitrary marker-summary responses in this form.

## Conceptual annotation-level MT model

For multiple traits,

$$
S=A\Gamma+E_A.
$$

Let the annotation-effect vector for annotation $k$ be

$$
\gamma_k
=
(\gamma_{k1},\ldots,\gamma_{kT})^\top.
$$

A conceptual MT prior can place annotation $k$ into trait-sharing patterns and
learn whether its posterior association is trait specific or shared.

This is distinct from the current genomic MT BayesR/BayesRC state models:
here the **observations are marker-level summaries** and the **predictors are
annotations**.

# Set-based empirical-Bayes inclusion probabilities

For binary annotation set $\mathcal S_k$, a smoothed empirical estimate of a
trait-specific inclusion probability is

$$
\widehat\pi_{k,t}
=
\frac{
a+
\sum_{j\in\mathcal S_k}
\widehat{\operatorname{PIP}}_{jt}
}{
2a+|\mathcal S_k|
},
$$

where $a>0$ is a symmetric pseudo-count.

For example, $a=1$ gives one prior pseudo-observation in each activity state.

```r
estimate_annotation_pi <- function(dm, sets, alpha = 1) {
  nt <- ncol(dm)
  K <- length(sets)

  pi_ann <- matrix(
    NA_real_,
    nrow = K,
    ncol = nt,
    dimnames = list(names(sets), colnames(dm))
  )

  for (k in seq_along(sets)) {
    idx <- sets[[k]]

    for (t in seq_len(nt)) {
      pi_ann[k, t] <-
        (alpha + sum(dm[idx, t])) /
        (2 * alpha + length(idx))
    }
  }

  pmin(pmax(pi_ann, 1e-8), 1 - 1e-8)
}
```

This construction is easiest to interpret for disjoint sets. For overlapping
annotations, assigning each set estimate directly to its member markers can
double-count information.

# Set-based empirical-Bayes effect scales

A signed allocation such as
$\widehat a_{g,k,t}^{(\mathrm{signed})}$ must not be assigned directly to a
Normal-prior variance. One nonnegative construction uses the within-set
quadratic defined above. Let

$$
m^{\mathrm{eff}}_{k,t}
=
\sum_{j\in\mathcal S_k}
\widehat{\operatorname{PIP}}_{jt}
$$

and choose a declared small threshold $\epsilon_m>0$. The threshold, any
positive fallback, and the shrinkage weight used below are non-unique
calibration choices, not consequences of the probability model. When
$m^{\mathrm{eff}}_{k,t}>\epsilon_m$, define

$$
\widehat\sigma_{b,k,t}^{2,\mathrm{within}}
=
\frac{
\widehat v_{g,k,t}^{(\mathrm{within})}
}{
m^{\mathrm{eff}}_{k,t}
}.
$$

When $m^{\mathrm{eff}}_{k,t}\le\epsilon_m$, the set does not identify a stable
data-derived effect scale. A declared positive fallback, such as a global prior
scale, should be used, or the set-specific update should be omitted. Silently
dividing by an arbitrary floor obscures that lack of information.

If the validated within-set quadratic is exactly zero, the fitted set-specific
genetic value has zero variance. A model requiring a strictly positive active
Normal-prior variance must likewise use a declared positive fallback or omit
the set-specific active component; it must not reinterpret a signed allocation
as the missing scale.

When the within-set operator is positive semidefinite, this is a nonnegative,
LD-dependent within-set-genetic-variance-per-expected-active-marker
calibration. It is not an identified average active-effect variance because its
numerator includes within-set LD cross-terms, and it is not an estimate of the
same object as the signed allocation.

A second theoretical construction targets average non-null effect squared:

$$
\widehat\sigma_{b,k,t}^{2,\mathrm{second}}
=
\frac{
\sum_{j\in\mathcal S_k}
\mathbb E(b_{jt}^2\mid\mathcal D)
}{
\sum_{j\in\mathcal S_k}
\operatorname{PIP}_{jt}
}.
$$

It is defined only when the denominator exceeds a declared positive threshold.
Otherwise the same fallback-or-omit rule is required. The numerator requires
posterior second moments, which may be computed from retained posterior draws;
it must not be approximated by squared posterior means without explicitly
changing the target. No current fit-object field is assumed here.

The two nonnegative constructions are not equivalent. The within-set quadratic
provides the LD-dependent calibration just described. When the required
posterior information is available, the posterior-second-moment ratio has a
more direct average non-null second-moment interpretation and does not include
LD cross-products.

A conceptual implementation is shown below. It accepts either one positive
fallback scale shared by all traits or one positive fallback per trait.

```r
estimate_annotation_vb_within <- function(
  b,
  pip,
  C_X,
  sets,
  n,
  fallback,
  min_eff = 1e-8,
  shrink = 0.5
) {
  if (!is.numeric(n) || length(n) != 1L || !is.finite(n) || n <= 0) {
    stop("`n` must be one finite, strictly positive common sample size.")
  }
  if (!is.numeric(min_eff) || length(min_eff) != 1L ||
      !is.finite(min_eff) || min_eff <= 0) {
    stop("`min_eff` must be one finite, strictly positive threshold.")
  }
  if (!is.numeric(shrink) || length(shrink) != 1L ||
      !is.finite(shrink) || shrink < 0 || shrink > 1) {
    stop("`shrink` must be one finite scalar between zero and one.")
  }
  if (!is.numeric(b) || !is.matrix(b) ||
      nrow(b) == 0L || ncol(b) == 0L || any(!is.finite(b))) {
    stop("`b` must be a nonempty finite numeric marker-by-trait matrix.")
  }
  if (!is.numeric(pip) || !is.matrix(pip) ||
      !identical(dim(b), dim(pip)) || any(!is.finite(pip)) ||
      any(pip < 0 | pip > 1)) {
    stop("`pip` must be a finite matrix in [0, 1] with the dimensions of `b`.")
  }
  if (!is.numeric(C_X) || !is.matrix(C_X) ||
      !identical(dim(C_X), c(nrow(b), nrow(b))) ||
      any(!is.finite(C_X)) ||
      !isTRUE(all.equal(C_X, t(C_X), tolerance = sqrt(.Machine$double.eps)))) {
    stop("`C_X` must be a finite symmetric marker-by-marker matrix aligned to `b`.")
  }
  if (!is.list(sets) || length(sets) == 0L) {
    stop("`sets` must be a nonempty list of marker-index vectors.")
  }

  valid_set <- vapply(sets, function(idx) {
    is.numeric(idx) && length(idx) > 0L && all(is.finite(idx)) &&
      all(idx == floor(idx)) && all(idx >= 1L & idx <= nrow(b)) &&
      !anyDuplicated(idx)
  }, logical(1))
  if (!all(valid_set)) {
    stop("Each set must contain unique integer marker indices within `b`.")
  }

  nt <- ncol(b)
  K <- length(sets)

  if (!is.numeric(fallback) || !(length(fallback) %in% c(1L, nt)) ||
      any(!is.finite(fallback)) || any(fallback <= 0)) {
    stop("`fallback` must contain one or one-per-trait finite positive scale.")
  }
  fallback <- rep(fallback, length.out = nt)

  vb_ann <- matrix(NA_real_, K, nt)
  vg_within <- matrix(NA_real_, K, nt)
  meff <- matrix(NA_real_, K, nt)

  rownames(vb_ann) <- rownames(vg_within) <-
    rownames(meff) <- names(sets)

  colnames(vb_ann) <- colnames(vg_within) <-
    colnames(meff) <- colnames(b)

  for (k in seq_along(sets)) {
    idx <- sets[[k]]
    C_set <- C_X[idx, idx, drop = FALSE]

    for (t in seq_len(nt)) {
      b_set <- b[idx, t]
      Cb_set <- drop(C_set %*% b_set)
      quad <- sum(b_set * Cb_set)
      quad_scale <- sum(abs(b_set * Cb_set))
      neff <- sum(pip[idx, t])

      if (!is.finite(quad) || !is.finite(quad_scale) || !is.finite(neff)) {
        stop("Within-set quadratics and effective marker counts must be finite.")
      }

      quad_tol <- sqrt(.Machine$double.eps) * max(1, quad_scale)
      if (quad < -quad_tol) {
        stop("A within-set quadratic is materially negative; validate `C_X` as positive semidefinite.")
      }
      vg <- max(quad, 0) / n

      vg_within[k, t] <- vg
      meff[k, t] <- neff
      vb_ann[k, t] <- if (
        neff <= min_eff || vg_within[k, t] == 0
      ) {
        fallback[t]
      } else {
        vg_within[k, t] / neff
      }
    }
  }

  vb_global <- colMeans(vb_ann, na.rm = TRUE)

  for (t in seq_len(nt)) {
    vb_ann[, t] <-
      shrink * vb_ann[, t] +
      (1 - shrink) * vb_global[t]
  }

  if (any(!is.finite(vb_ann)) || any(vb_ann <= 0)) {
    stop("Calibrated prior variances must be finite and strictly positive.")
  }

  list(vb = vb_ann, vg_within = vg_within, meff = meff)
}
```

This illustration assumes one common scalar sample size `n` across traits and
that `C_X` has already been validated as positive semidefinite and aligned to
the marker order in `b`; the code also checks its dimensions, finiteness, and
symmetry. The `max(quad, 0)` operation is only a guard against negligible
floating-point error after that validation; it is not a repair for a materially
indefinite operator. Because $0\leq\texttt{shrink}\leq1$, the final shrinkage
step is a convex combination of strictly positive scales. The chosen
`min_eff`, fallback values, and shrinkage weight remain non-unique calibration
decisions.

# From annotation effects to fixed marker-specific probability priors

For overlapping annotations, a fitted annotation model can be transformed into
marker-specific probability information.

Let $\widehat\gamma_t$ denote estimated annotation effects for trait $t$.
A conceptual linear predictor is

$$
\eta^{(P)}_{jt}
=
\mu_{\pi,t}
+
A_j\widehat\gamma_t.
$$

Then

$$
\pi_{jt}^{\mathrm{EB}}
=
\operatorname{logit}^{-1}
\left(
\eta^{(P)}_{jt}
\right).
$$

The superscript `EB` emphasizes that this is an empirical-Bayes prior
constructed from a previous analysis.

If the goal is to redistribute prior inclusion probability around a baseline
$\pi_t^{(0)}$, a centered construction is

$$
\widetilde\eta^{(P)}_{jt}
=
A_j\widehat\gamma_t
-
\frac{1}{M}
\sum_{\ell=1}^{M}
A_\ell\widehat\gamma_t,
$$

followed by

$$
\operatorname{logit}
\left(
\pi_{jt}^{\mathrm{EB}}
\right)
=
\operatorname{logit}
\left(
\pi_t^{(0)}
\right)
+
\widetilde\eta^{(P)}_{jt}.
$$

A conceptual implementation is:

```r
derive_pi_marker <- function(
  A,
  gamma,
  base_pi,
  cap = c(1e-8, 0.05)
) {
  A <- as.matrix(A)
  gamma <- as.matrix(gamma)

  eta <- A %*% gamma
  eta <- sweep(eta, 2, colMeans(eta), "-")
  eta <- sweep(eta, 2, qlogis(base_pi), "+")

  pi_marker <- plogis(eta)

  pmin(pmax(pi_marker, cap[1]), cap[2])
}
```

The clipping above belongs to this empirical fixed-prior construction. It
should not be confused with the canonical LV variance model or with every
future probability provider.

Current ST CSR BayesC can accept fixed marker-specific probability information
through its qualified fixed-marker annotation route. Exact public argument and
preprocessing contracts are documented outside this conceptual page.

# From annotation effects to fixed marker-specific variance priors

A parallel empirical construction can be used for marker-specific effect
variance.

Let

$$
q_{jt}^{\mathrm{EB}}
=
\exp
\left(
\widetilde\eta^{(Q)}_{jt}
\right),
$$

where

$$
\widetilde\eta^{(Q)}_{jt}
=
A_j\widehat\theta_t
-
\frac{1}{M}
\sum_{\ell=1}^{M}
A_\ell\widehat\theta_t.
$$

Then a marker-specific active-effect variance can be written as

$$
v_{b,jt}^{\mathrm{EB}}
=
v_{b,t}^{(0)}
q_{jt}^{\mathrm{EB}}.
$$

This is a conceptual empirical-Bayes construction. It is **not** the same
statistical model as the current learned log-variance LV model:

- the coefficients $\widehat\theta_t$ here are estimated in a separate stage
  and then treated as fixed;
- the transformation may be clipped for robustness;
- current LV learns $\theta$ jointly with the genomic marker model under its
  own preprocessing and Gaussian prior;
- LV uses one canonical learned $Q$ engine rather than this historical
  two-stage plug-in construction.

A conceptual implementation is:

```r
derive_vb_marker <- function(
  A,
  theta,
  global_vb,
  cap = c(0.25, 4)
) {
  A <- as.matrix(A)
  theta <- as.matrix(theta)

  eta <- A %*% theta
  eta <- sweep(eta, 2, colMeans(eta), "-")

  mult <- exp(eta)
  mult <- pmin(pmax(mult, cap[1]), cap[2])

  vb_marker <- sweep(mult, 2, global_vb, "*")

  pmax(vb_marker, 1e-12)
}
```

Current ST CSR BayesC can consume fixed marker variance multipliers through the
fixed-marker route. Current BayesC-LV and BayesR-LV instead learn the $Q$
architecture jointly and are described in
[Annotation-Informed Priors](annotation_priors.qmd).

# Using fixed empirical priors in a second genomic fit

A generic second-stage BayesC-style prior can be written

$$
d_{jt}
\sim
\operatorname{Bernoulli}
\left(
\pi_{jt}^{\mathrm{EB}}
\right),
$$

and

$$
b_{jt}\mid d_{jt}=1
\sim
N
\left(
0,
v_{b,t}^{(0)}
q_{jt}^{\mathrm{EB}}
\right).
$$

The empirical probability architecture and empirical variance architecture
enter different parts of the marker conditional.

The generic BayesC marker-update mathematics is given in
[Annotation-Informed Priors](annotation_priors.qmd). It is deliberately not
duplicated here.

A second-stage empirical-Bayes fit therefore uses the first analysis to
construct fixed prior inputs, then evaluates a new genomic posterior
conditional on those fixed inputs.

## Important uncertainty distinction

If $\widehat\gamma_t$ or $\widehat\theta_t$ is estimated from a first-stage
posterior and then treated as fixed, the second-stage posterior is conditional
on those estimates.

It does not automatically integrate over uncertainty in the annotation model.

This can lead to overconfident inference if the empirical prior is estimated
from the same data and the first-stage uncertainty is substantial.

# Cross-fitting and data reuse

If the same phenotype data are used to:

1. estimate genomic marker evidence;
2. estimate annotation effects from that marker evidence; and
3. refit the same markers with the annotation-informed prior,

then evidence can be reused.

A more conservative design is chromosome-wise or block-wise cross-fitting.

For chromosome $c$:

1. estimate annotation effects from markers outside chromosome $c$;
2. construct priors for chromosome $c$ from those out-of-fold estimates;
3. fit or evaluate chromosome $c$ using the resulting prior.

Conceptually:

```r
for (chr in chromosomes) {
  # Estimate annotation model without chr.
  # Derive priors for markers on chr.
  # Fit/evaluate chr under those out-of-fold priors.
}
```

Cross-fitting does not solve every problem:

- LD can extend across nominal folds;
- annotations may have highly uneven prevalence across chromosomes;
- hyperparameters can still be estimated globally;
- the final target differs from a single fully joint hierarchical posterior.

Nevertheless, it reduces direct reuse of each marker's own posterior evidence
when constructing its prior.

# Conceptual MT empirical-Bayes extensions

The following sections describe **research-stage** extensions for using
first-stage posterior summaries to inform multi-trait sharing or covariance
priors.

They are not descriptions of current ordinary MT BayesR or MT BayesRC
parameterization.

## Empirical sharing-pattern responsibilities

Suppose one wishes to approximate a probability that marker $j$ follows a
particular binary activity pattern

$$
a_p\in\{0,1\}^{T}
$$

from marginal first-stage PIPs.

A simple product construction is

$$
w_{jp}
=
\prod_{t=1}^{T}
\widehat{\operatorname{PIP}}_{jt}^{[a_p]_t}
\left(
1-\widehat{\operatorname{PIP}}_{jt}
\right)^{1-[a_p]_t}.
$$

This treats the trait-specific marginal activity probabilities as independent
when constructing the responsibility. That is a strong approximation.

For annotation set $\mathcal S_k$, a smoothed pattern probability could then be
written

$$
\widehat H_{k,p}^{\mathrm{EB}}
=
\frac{
a_p^{(0)}
+
\sum_{j\in\mathcal S_k}w_{jp}
}{
\sum_\ell a_\ell^{(0)}
+
|\mathcal S_k|
}.
$$

This is a conceptual empirical-Bayes summary, not a current MT BayesR `joint_pi`
update and not the current MT BayesRC global $H$ update.

## Annotation-dependent sharing as a research extension

For overlapping annotations, one could instead define marker-specific pattern
probabilities through a multinomial model:

$$
H_{jp}
=
\frac{
\exp
\left(
\zeta_p+A_j\delta_p
\right)
}{
\sum_\ell
\exp
\left(
\zeta_\ell+A_j\delta_\ell
\right)
}.
$$

This would make trait sharing annotation dependent.

Such a model is **not currently implemented** in `sblr`. It belongs to future
research on annotation-dependent $H$ and must not be confused with:

- ordinary MT BayesR's full `joint_pi` simplex; or
- current MT BayesRC's global conditional $H$.

# Conceptual annotation-informed MT covariance

One may also ask whether first-stage annotation summaries could inform the
marker-effect covariance $V_b$ of a later MT analysis.

Let

$$
\widehat\gamma_k
\in
\mathbb R^T
$$

be an estimated annotation-effect vector across traits. A weighted descriptive
covariance is

$$
\widehat V_{b,\mathrm{ann}}
=
\frac{
\sum_{k=1}^{K}
w_k
\widehat\gamma_k
\widehat\gamma_k^\top
}{
\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_k
}.
$$

For example, $w_k$ might reflect an annotation-level inclusion probability.

This is best viewed as an **initialization or empirical prior construction**.
The covariance of annotation-level regression coefficients is not automatically
the same estimand as the covariance of genomic marker effects.

A conceptual R sketch is:

```r
estimate_Vb_from_annotation_model <- function(
  gamma,
  dm,
  ridge = 1e-8
) {
  gamma <- as.matrix(gamma)
  w <- pmax(apply(dm, 1, max), 1e-6)

  Vb <- crossprod(gamma * sqrt(w)) / sum(w)
  Vb <- 0.5 * (Vb + t(Vb))
  diag(Vb) <- pmax(diag(Vb), ridge)

  Vb
}
```

Current `sblr` does not implement annotation-dependent $V_b$. A matrix derived
this way could at most serve as a fixed/initial externally constructed
quantity under a separately validated workflow.

# Regional warm starts and conditional analyses

First-stage ST posterior means can also be used as initialization for a later
regional analysis.

For marker $j$ and trait $t$,

$$
b_{jt}^{(0)}
=
\widehat b_{jt}^{\,\mathrm{ST}}
$$

is a natural warm start.

Candidate regions can be prioritized using criteria such as

$$
\max_t
\widehat{\operatorname{PIP}}_{jt}
>
\tau,
$$

followed by LD expansion.

A residual score initialized from the complete warm-start effect vector is

$$
r_t^{(0)}
=
X^\top y_t
-
X^\top Xb_t^{(0)}.
$$

Updating only a selected region while keeping the remainder fixed changes the
inferential problem. It is therefore a conditional or sensitivity analysis,
not automatically the same posterior as the original genome-wide model.

This distinction is developed further in
[Fine-Mapping and Credible Sets](fine_mapping.qmd).

# Historical direct in-sampler annotation sketches

::: {.callout-warning title="Historical / research-stage material"}
The constructions in this section are retained because they explain ideas that
motivated parts of the annotation-prior architecture. They are **not** the
current implementation plan.

Current learned probability and variance architectures are documented in
[Annotation-Informed Priors](annotation_priors.qmd):

- learned logistic provides a current ST CSR BayesC probability mechanism and
  also contains a historical learned variance half;
- LV is the canonical learned $Q$ mechanism for current ST CSR/block-eigen
  BayesC/BayesR;
- probit stick is the current learned BayesRC component-probability mechanism;
- simultaneous newly learned $P+Q$, annotation-dependent $H$, and
  annotation-dependent $V_b$ require separate validation.
:::

## Generic direct ST prior

A generic annotation-informed BayesC prior can be written

$$
d_j
\sim
\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_j),
$$

$$
b_j\mid d_j=1
\sim
N(0,v_bq_j),
$$

with, for example,

$$
\operatorname{logit}(\pi_j)
=
\mu_\pi
+
\widetilde A^{(P)}_j\eta_\pi,
$$

and

$$
\log q_j
=
\widetilde A^{(Q)}_j\eta_Q.
$$

The processed designs
$\widetilde A^{(P)}$ and $\widetilde A^{(Q)}$ are written separately because
probability and variance providers need not use identical preprocessing.

This generic equation is useful architecture notation. It should not be read as
a claim that arbitrary simultaneous learned $P+Q$ composition is currently
supported.

## Fixed versus learned annotation coefficients

Two conceptually different choices are:

- estimate annotation coefficients externally and treat them as fixed in the
  genomic sampler;
- assign priors to annotation coefficients and update them jointly with marker
  effects.

The first choice is an empirical-Bayes model conditional on a fixed
annotation-derived prior.

The second is a fully joint hierarchical model and can have very different
posterior dependence and MCMC behavior.

Current `sblr` contains model-specific examples of both ideas, but they should
not be collapsed into one generic sampler identity.

## Why direct joint learning is harder

When annotation coefficients are learned jointly with marker states, feedback
can occur:

$$
\text{annotation coefficients}
\longrightarrow
\text{marker prior}
\longrightarrow
\text{marker states/effects}
\longrightarrow
\text{annotation coefficients}.
$$

This feedback can be scientifically appropriate, but it can also generate
strong posterior dependence, weak identifiability, and slow mixing.

The known SBayesRC alpha/occupancy behavior is one example of why a mathematically
valid conditional update does not guarantee good joint posterior exploration.

# Recommended empirical-Bayes workflow

A defensible staged workflow is:

## Stage 1: fit the genomic model

Fit the chosen ST or MT genomic model and retain:

- posterior mean marker effects;
- PIPs;
- component probabilities where relevant;
- residual-score information where required for LD-aware contributions; and
- convergence diagnostics.

## Stage 2: summarize annotation signal

Calculate quantities such as:

- set-specific genomic contributions;
- PIP enrichment;
- annotation-level conditional regressions; or
- an annotation-level Bayesian model.

## Stage 3: construct the empirical prior

Depending on the scientific goal, construct:

- fixed marker-specific inclusion probabilities;
- fixed marker-specific variance multipliers;
- fixed group-level priors;
- an externally informed covariance initialization; or
- a cross-fitted prior for another marker set.

## Stage 4: refit under the declared prior

Fit the genomic model again while explicitly recording that the prior was
estimated empirically.

If the prior was estimated from the same data, report the data-reuse issue and
consider cross-fitting or external validation.

# Interpreting empirical-Bayes priors

An empirical prior is not simply "biological truth supplied to the model."

It is a statistical transformation of evidence from:

- the first-stage genomic model;
- the chosen posterior summary;
- the annotation design;
- any smoothing or shrinkage;
- centering/normalization;
- clipping or bounding;
- the LD representation; and
- any cross-fitting or data-splitting procedure.

For example, a fixed prior probability

$$
\pi_{jt}^{\mathrm{EB}}
$$

constructed from first-stage PIPs inherits uncertainty and model dependence
from those PIPs.

Likewise, a fixed variance multiplier

$$
q_{jt}^{\mathrm{EB}}
$$

derived from fitted effects is not a direct measurement of biological effect
variance.

These distinctions should be explicit when comparing empirical-Bayes models to
fully hierarchical annotation models.

# Causal interpretation and hypothesis generation

Annotation-informed BLR can provide evidence for:

- genetic association;
- trait sharing;
- annotation enrichment;
- effect-size architecture; and
- plausible biological mechanisms.

It does not, by itself, establish intervention-level causal relationships.

For example,

$$
\Pr(d_{jt}=1\mid\mathcal D)
$$

is a posterior activity probability under the fitted model. It is not a causal
effect of annotation membership on the trait.

Likewise, a conceptual annotation-level posterior such as

$$
\Pr(
\text{annotation }k\text{ contributes to a marker-level response}
\mid
\mathcal D
)
$$

is evidence about an annotation model, not proof that changing the annotation
would change the phenotype.

## Genetic sharing versus causal direction

Suppose a region shows evidence that the same marker is active for two traits.
That can be compatible with several mechanisms, including:

$$
G\longrightarrow t_1\longrightarrow t_2,
$$

$$
G\longrightarrow t_2\longrightarrow t_1,
$$

or horizontal pleiotropy,

$$
G\longrightarrow t_1
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
G\longrightarrow t_2.
$$

A shared genetic-effect pattern does not distinguish these causal structures.

## Fine-mapping and colocalization

Fine-mapping can narrow the set of marker explanations within a locus, but the
current `sblr` credible-set helpers are marginal-PIP post-processing procedures,
not effect-specific causal-configuration models.

See [Fine-Mapping and Credible Sets](fine_mapping.qmd).

If two traits show a shared regional signal, colocalization can provide
additional evidence about whether their association patterns are compatible
with one shared causal variant. That evidence is stronger than simple regional
sharing, but still depends on the assumptions of the colocalization model.

## Mendelian randomization

Mendelian randomization can address directional hypotheses such as

$$
x\longrightarrow y
$$

under instrumental-variable assumptions.

Annotation-aware BLR can help prioritize or classify potential instruments, but
it does not make those assumptions true. Broad pleiotropic marker evidence may
instead be a warning that exclusion-restriction assumptions need particular
scrutiny.

## Appropriate role of annotation-aware BLR

A careful interpretation is:

> Annotation-informed BLR identifies markers, regions, annotations, and
> trait-sharing structures that are enriched for genetic evidence under the
> fitted model. These results can prioritize biological mechanisms and
> downstream causal analyses, but causal interpretation requires additional
> assumptions or external evidence.

Complementary analyses may include:

- denser regional fine-mapping;
- colocalization with molecular QTL data;
- Mendelian randomization;
- mediation analysis;
- perturbation experiments; and
- independent functional validation.

# Practical reporting

When reporting an empirical-Bayes annotation analysis, record:

- the first-stage genomic model and likelihood operator;
- the posterior marker summary used as the annotation response;
- the annotation matrix and preprocessing;
- whether annotations overlap;
- the empirical-prior transformation;
- centering, shrinkage, and clipping;
- whether the same data were reused;
- whether cross-fitting or external data were used;
- whether second-stage prior coefficients were fixed or learned;
- which quantities are current implemented features versus conceptual
  extensions; and
- sensitivity to the annotation model and LD representation.
